How RainSignal works

RainSignal takes yesterday's weather measurements from 44 Australian towns and estimates the chance of rain the next day. This page explains where the numbers come from, what they mean, and where they stop being useful. It starts in plain language and gets more technical as it goes.

What RainSignal actually does

Every day, weather stations around Australia record things like temperature, humidity, air pressure and wind. RainSignal collects those measurements, waits until a day is complete, and feeds that finished day into a computer program that has studied eighteen years of Australian weather. The program returns one number: the chance that more than one millimetre of rain falls at that town the next day.

That is the whole product. It does not forecast temperature, storms, or anything beyond the single yes-or-no question of rain, and it only knows about the 44 towns it was trained on.

Where the weather information comes from

Observations come from the Bureau of Meteorology, Australia's national weather agency, through the file service the Bureau provides for automated access. RainSignal reads seven files covering every state, several times a day, and keeps only the stations it needs.

These are observations: measurements of weather that has already happened. They are not the Bureau's forecasts. RainSignal never uses a forecast as an input, because a prediction built on someone else's prediction is not a prediction of its own.

How a prediction is produced

  1. Collect. Current readings are fetched and checked. A reading outside a physically possible range is thrown away rather than corrected, because a corrected value looks exactly like a real one.
  2. Wait for the day to finish. A day is only usable once every hour of it has passed in that town's own time zone. This matters more than it sounds: a day still in progress would mean guessing at its own totals.
  3. Assemble. The day's readings are arranged into the same shape the program learned from: the temperature, humidity, pressure and wind at 9am and 3pm, the day's high and low, its rainfall, and its strongest gust.
  4. Estimate. That row goes through the frozen program, which returns a probability between 0 and 100.
  5. Publish. The number appears on the map with the date it was measured and the date it refers to.

Nothing in this chain retrains or adjusts the program. It was trained once, measured once, and frozen before this site existed, which is what makes the accuracy figures on the Analytics page meaningful.

What the number means

A reading of 70 means: on days that looked like this one, at this town, it rained about 70 times in 100.

It is not a promise, and it is not a percentage of the sky or of the day. A 30% day that turns out wet is not necessarily a mistake — roughly three in ten of those days are supposed to be wet. You can only judge these numbers over many days, which is exactly how they were tested.

RainSignal deliberately shows a probability rather than a yes-or-no answer. Turning a probability into a label means choosing a cut-off, and that choice silently decides whether the tool would rather miss rain or cry wolf. That decision belongs to whoever is reading, not to us.

Why some towns show no estimate

The program needs a complete day. If a station did not report some of the measurements — its 3pm humidity, say, or its rainfall total — RainSignal shows no number for that town and says which measurements were missing.

Filling those gaps with plausible guesses would produce a number that looks exactly as confident as a real one, and there would be no way for a reader to tell the difference. Withholding it is the honest option.

Five of the 49 towns in the historical record have no live weather station at all, so they never appear on the map.

What it can and cannot tell you

It can

  • Give a reasonable sense of whether tomorrow looks wet or dry at one of its towns.
  • Tell you how well it has performed in that particular town before.
  • Show you the actual measurements its answer was built from.

It cannot

  • Replace the Bureau of Meteorology. For warnings, flooding or any decision that matters, use bom.gov.au.
  • Say how much rain will fall, or when in the day.
  • Say anything about a place it has no station for.
  • See further than one day ahead.

The words you will see

These terms appear in the Technical detail sections. Each is given plainly first, then precisely.

Probability
Plainly: how likely rain is, out of 100. Precisely: the model's estimated conditional probability that tomorrow's rainfall exceeds 1 mm, given today's observations at that station.
Recall
Plainly: of the days it really rained, how many the model spotted. Precisely: true positives divided by all actual positives. RainSignal's model has a recall of about 0.55 nationally, so it spots roughly 55 of every 100 rainy days.
Precision
Plainly: when it warned of rain, how often it was right. Precisely: true positives divided by all predicted positives. About 0.78 nationally, so roughly four out of five rain warnings were correct.
F1
Plainly: a single score that balances the two above, so a model cannot look good by only chasing one. Precisely: the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The harmonic mean is used rather than a plain average because it punishes a model that is excellent at one and poor at the other.
Accuracy, and why we do not lead with it
Plainly: the share of all days it got right — which sounds like the obvious measure and is nearly useless here. Precisely: rain falls on about 22% of days, so always answering "no rain" scores 78% accuracy while catching no rain at all. This is called class imbalance, and it is why precision, recall and F1 carry the judgement instead.
ROC-AUC
Plainly: how good the model is at ranking wet days above dry ones, where 0.5 is a coin toss and 1.0 is perfect. Precisely: the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve — the probability that a randomly chosen rainy day is scored higher than a randomly chosen dry one. RainSignal's model scores about 0.90.
Calibration
Plainly: whether a 70 really means 70. Precisely: the agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies. Measured by expected calibration error; RainSignal's model scores 0.0120, which is what makes it defensible to publish its output as a probability at all.
Reliability (the "how reliable" map)
Plainly: how well the model has done in one particular town. Precisely: that station's F1 on the held-out test set. It ranges from 0.40 to 0.78 across the 44 towns and correlates 0.47 with how often it rains there — the model is weakest where rain is rarest, because there are fewer examples of rain to learn from.

How it was tested

The program studied 187,121 days and was then judged on 80,196 days it had never seen. Those days were set aside before any tuning, and were looked at once, at the end. Tuning against a test set turns it into a practice set, and the score stops meaning anything.

Four programs were compared on identical data. A neural network scored best and is the one RainSignal serves, though it beat a much simpler random forest by only about seven days in a thousand.

Technical detail

Target: RainTomorrow, defined as more than 1 mm of rainfall on the following day, from the weatherAUS record originally distributed with the rattle package.

Features: 16 same-day observations plus five derived terms — a cyclical month encoding, the day's temperature range, and the 9am-to-3pm changes in pressure and humidity. Sunshine, evaporation and cloud were dropped because their absence is structural rather than random: 19 of 49 stations never record sunshine at all, so imputing it would write one national median into every row of those stations.

A column named RISK_MM was removed after testing showed it to be the next day's rainfall recorded on the current day. Thresholding it at 1 mm reproduced the target on 100.0000% of 267,317 rows. Any model given it reads the answer rather than predicting it.

Preprocessing — median and most-frequent imputation, standardisation and one-hot encoding — is fitted on the training split alone and frozen. Live observations pass through that same fitted preprocessing, so a gap in the live data is filled exactly as it was during training, and nowhere else.

Model: a three-layer network (128, 64, 32) with dropout 0.3, early stopping on validation loss. Test-set accuracy 0.8666, precision 0.7815, recall 0.5482, F1 0.6444, ROC-AUC 0.8994, Brier 0.0966, expected calibration error 0.0120. Its best decision threshold sits near 0.31 rather than 0.5, which is a further reason no yes-or-no label is imposed.

Everything above is reproducible from the notebook and code in the project repository.

RainSignal is a student project built for PRT565 at Charles Darwin University. Observations are reproduced from the Bureau of Meteorology. The chance shown is produced by a machine-learning model and is not a Bureau forecast.
